newsitem.title: USA: Gold soars as U.S. stocks, bonds, dollar fall.
newsitem.headline: Gold soars as U.S. stocks, bonds, dollar fall.

text.p: Gold prices jumped Friday, boosted by a sharp slide in stocks, bonds and the dollar.

"The gold market was looking for a reason to recover after seeing 12-year lows last month and the selloff in financial markets provided the impetus," Chase Manhattan managing director for global commodities Dinsa Mehta said.
"The weakness in the dollar was especially significant as the dollar's strength has been a factor in gold's weakness of late," he said.
Gold for December rose $4.60 to $330.40 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange after hitting $332 during the session, its highest level in a week.

"Gold is still only about $10 an ounce off its 12-year lows, but the bullion market has absorbed huge supply in recent weeks and there is a feeling that today could be the start of some asset price deflation, so my own feeling is gold could edge higher from here," Mehta said.
The Dow Jones industrial average slid 156.78 points to 8,031.22 and the 30-year U.S. Treasury fell 1-7/16, or $14.38 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.64 percent from 6.53 percent Thursday.
The dollar posted its biggest losses against major currencies in three months, falling to 1.8452 German marks from 1.8690 marks late on Thursday, and to 114.80 Japanese yen from 118.43 yen.
Crude oil prices fell after the market was dealt a one-two punch by sharp losses in gasoline prices and news that Iraqi oil exports will restart next week.
"There was just a bloodbath in the gasoline market, and the Iraqi news just added to it," one trader said.
September crude fell 55 cents to $19.54 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange, capping a 76-cent loss for the week.
September gasoline fell 2.34 cents to 61.99 cents a gallon and September heating oil finished 1.01 cents lower at 54.29 cents a gallon.
"The market is acting as if the exports will arrive imminently when exports may not show up here for a couple of weeks," said Pat Hughes, analyst with Chevron Corp. in Walnut, Creek, Calif.

Next week, U.S. oil company Coastal Corp. is expected to load 4 million barrels of Iraqi oil, half Basrah grade and half Kirkuk grade, traders said. Trading firm Bayoil is expected to load more than 2 million barrels.
Due to changes in the price structure, Iraqi Kirkuk oil will flow to the U.S. for the first time since the 1990 Gulf War, implying more crude import volume to the U.S.
On Friday, the U.N. formally approved Iraq's oil price formula, allowing Iraq to sell oil for first time since May.
Still, dealers were uncertain about how much oil Iraq will export under a second six month instalment of its "oil for food" deal with the U.N.
Soybean prices closed mostly higher as traders bet weekend rains would again bypass key growing areas in central Illinois and Indiana.

"People got the weather hives," said Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc. "One of the forecasters reduced the precip forecast for Illinois and (prices) went nuts. We all got really scared and broke out in rashes and said it doesn't look like it's going to rain."
Illinois and Indiana are among the leading soybean growing states. There has been growing concern that dry conditions will hurt crops in those states.
Soybeans for November delivery rose 9 cents to $6.37-1/2 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.
